message.content:
Conductivity and heat storage are two different things. Conductivity describes how quickly heat moves through a material. Aluminum excels at this, so a thin aluminum pan heats fast and spreads heat evenly. Staying hot, however, depends on how much heat the pan has stored, and that depends mostly on mass. A typical cast-iron skillet weighs five or six pounds, while a thin aluminum pan might weigh one. Even though aluminum stores more heat per pound than iron, the heavy skillet holds far more heat in total.

Picture searing four cold steaks. When they hit a thin aluminum pan, they pull heat out faster than the burner can replace it. The surface temperature drops, the meat releases moisture, and the steaks steam and turn gray. Drop the same steaks into a preheated cast-iron skillet and the large reserve of stored heat keeps the surface hot enough to brown them into a deep crust. That same reserve is why cast iron stays warm on the table long after you turn off the stove.

The comparison has a limitation. It really pits a heavy pan against a light one rather than iron against aluminum. A thick aluminum pan of similar weight would hold comparable heat and spread it more evenly, while cast iron tends to develop hot spots over the burner.
